text.description:
The Vasa Museum (Vasamuseet) sits on the island of Djurgården and houses the 64-gun warship Vasa, which sank on her maiden voyage in 1628. It is the only almost fully intact 17th-century ship ever salvaged. The museum opened on 15 June 1990, and from outside it is easy to pick out. A large copper roof carries stylised masts that show how tall Vasa stood when fully rigged. Some of the walls are clad in wooden panels painted dark red, blue, tar black, ochre yellow and dark green, which gives you colour and texture to work with.

The best outdoor photo is from the waterfront edge of Galärparken, a free, leafy park right beside the museum. From there you see the roofline and masts with boats moored in the harbour in front. Four other museum ships lie in that harbour: the ice breaker Sankt Erik, the lightvessel Finngrundet, the torpedo boat Spica and the rescue boat Bernhard Ingelsson. They make good foreground interest. Leave a little space around the roof and masts so the shape reads clearly. Photographing the ship itself means going inside, where it can be seen from six levels. Check the official site for photo rules and ticket details before you go.
text.access_note: Galärparken is a free public park, but entry to the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Head for the island of Djurgården in Stockholm and look for the Vasa Museum. From there the museum's middle is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: On the island of Djurgården in Stockholm, on the harbour waterfront.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the roof to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out the copper. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, because telephoto and the default lens (1x) give quite different results here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the roof and the water. Midday sun can cause glare off the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole roofline with the boats in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the roof and masts will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the masts and roof detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Galärparken (waterfront edge of the park, facing the museum). The museum's striking copper roof and the boats moored in the harbour in front of it. The museum lies to the north-west. From here the photo shows the museum's copper roof and the boats moored in the harbour in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the roofline along the upper third, with the moored boats along the bottom. Keep the phone level so the masts stand upright. If you want an alternative, the museum's front exterior shows the copper bowsprit above the roof, with the harbour and vintage ships behind.

spots.name: Gamla Stan and Stortorget
spots.label: Stortorget

text.description: Stortorget, the "Grand Square", is the oldest square in Stockholm and the historic heart of Gamla Stan, the old town. It never was a grand showpiece. The buildings around it were added gradually and a little haphazardly, which gives the square an uneven, lived-in look that suits photos well. The northern side is taken up by the Stock Exchange Building (Börshuset), designed by Erik Palmstedt and built between 1773 and 1776. Its rounded corner and lantern-style cupola are easy to spot. Today it houses the Swedish Academy and the Nobel Museum. In the square itself there is an old well, also by Palmstedt. Around the edges you will find tall, colourful town houses. One of them, number 3 (Grillska huset), has cloverleaf-shaped gables added in 1718 and a blue façade. The square is known for its Christmas market, when it is busy and full of colour. For a good photo, include a little of the cobbled ground in the foreground so the viewer feels the size of the space. Then let the façades fill the rest. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the buildings stay straight. If you want a close-up, look for the gables and the rounded corner of the Stock Exchange Building. Right next to it: Stockholm Cathedral (Storkyrkan). Right next to it: German Church.
text.access_note: Stortorget is a public square; the Nobel Museum and other buildings around it may have their own opening rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Head for Gamla Stan, the old town in central Stockholm, and continue on foot. The square lies in the middle of the island. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Stortorget is in the middle of Gamla Stan, the old town in central Stockholm, on the plateau of the island of Stadsholmen. The Stock Exchange Building stands on its northern side.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and the colours do not wash out. In the evening or at the Christmas market, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in the frame. In the evening, with the lights on, the square looks warmer, and night mode works well then.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the width of the square and the façades in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the gables and the cupola.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with the vertical lines to keep them straight. Keep a strip of cobbles at the bottom of the frame for depth. Then take a second shot with the telephoto, focused on the Stock Exchange Building or a single gabled house.

spots.alt: Gamla Stan and Stortorget, Stockholm: the oldest square in Stockholm and the historic heart of Gamla Stan. Photo spot

spots.name: ABBA The Museum
spots.label: ABBA The Museum

text.description:
ABBA The Museum is an interactive exhibition about the Swedish pop band, on the island of Djurgården in Stockholm. It opened in May 2013 and sits in a building near the Gröna Lund theme park. It is the permanent home of the ABBAWORLD exhibition, which toured Europe and Australia in 2009–2011, and it holds stage costumes donated by the band members. Inside you will find a recreation of the Polar Studio, a section styled on Brighton at the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest, and Benny's self-playing piano, which is linked to the one in his home.

For a phone photographer, the outside of the building is the easy, reliable shot. It is a big, simple subject that sits well in a wide frame, and Djurgården gives it a relaxed, leisurely setting. Find a spot outside with a clear view of the facade and photograph the building as a record of your visit, perhaps with a friend in the foreground. Step back a few paces to fit more of it in, and switch on gridlines so the walls stay straight.

Inside, photography rules can differ from room to room, so look out for signs and check the official site before you go. If photos are allowed, the costumes and studio recreations make good close-up details.
text.access_note: The museum is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules inside.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for the best way to reach Djurgården. Once there, head for Gröna Lund and look for the museum in a building near it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: On the island of Djurgården in central Stockholm, in a building near the Gröna Lund theme park.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls do not turn washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in even light is easiest. Earlier in the day it is likely to be quieter. If you come in the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building as a whole. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for signs and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Find a spot outside the building with a clear view of the facade, and take a few steps back to fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with them so the walls look straight. Keep your phone level, as tilting it makes the building lean. If the area is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or include a few people for a sense of scale.
